In multimodal sentiment analysis a concrete example is that multiple speakers in a dataset who happen to wear glasses also happen to express negative sentiment; a model can learn the rule that glasses predict negative sentiment and still perform well on held-out data from the same distribution even though this association is a dataset collection artifact that would fail in the real world. In VQA a parallel phenomenon emerges: because approximately 80 percent of bananas in the training set are yellow a language-only model that ignores the image entirely answers yellow to any banana color question and is correct most of the time. When the same model is tested on a green banana it still predicts yellow demonstrating that it learned a statistical shortcut from the language distribution rather than genuinely reasoning about visual content. In both cases models can achieve strong benchmark numbers while learning non-causal associations.

This can lead to models learning these spurious associations rather than the true underlying sentiment, resulting in poor generalization to new data.

In both sentiment analysis and Visual Question Answering (VQA) research, confounding factors manifest similarly. In sentiment analysis, the presence of certain physical traits (like smiling or frowning) can be misinterpreted as indicators of sentiment, while in VQA, models might rely on superficial features in images (like the color of an object) rather than understanding the context of the question. Both areas face the challenge of ensuring that models learn to focus on relevant, person-independent features while minimizing the influence of these confounding factors. This is crucial for developing unbiased and effective models in multimodal contexts.
